newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Plans progress for Schengen's Nordic expansion.
newsitem.headline: Plans progress for Schengen's Nordic expansion.

text.p: The Schengen Executive Committee on Thursday firmed up plans to admit the five countries of the Nordic Passport Union by the end of the year.

The ministers reached political agreement on full membership terms for European Union members Denmark, Sweden and Finland, and associate membership for Norway and Iceland, which are outside the EU, Luxembourg Justice Minister Marc Fischbach said.
"It was possible to reach a political agreement among all the delegations on the terms," Fischbach told a news conference.

Seven full members of the zone -- France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Portugal, Spain and Germany -- dropped airport passport checks for each others' nationals on March 26, 1995, when Schengen came into effect.

The accord, named after the Luxembourg town in which it was signed, quickly fell short of expectations after France, in deep disagreement with the Netherlands over drugs policy, refused to drop land border checks as planned on July 1, 1995.

Fischbach said France had indicated on the sidelines of the meeting that it would take several months to finalise an accord with the Hague on drugs policy which would allow it to drop the land border checks with Belgium and Luxembourg.
Paris accuses the two countries of being transit points for Dutch drugs.
The agreements with the five Nordic countries will now be finally signed when the ministers next meet in Luxembourg on December 19, Fischbach said.
Talks had been complicated as the two non-EU members, Norway and Iceland, will have to apply some parts of EU legislation, for example on asylum and visa policy.
Three other signatories who are not yet fully implementing the accord -- Italy, Austria and Greece -- vowed at the meeting to be fully on board in 1997, although a specific date was not set.
They have to pass data protection laws and make sure their external borders are properly policed.
The expansion has financial implications for the Schengen accord.

Its Schengen Information System computer system -- seen as essential to the common fight against crime -- was only conceived for five countries and will now have to admit 15, FIschbach said, adding a second computer might be necessary.
The computer contains, among other things, lists of people considered undesireable, to help in processing visa applications and preventing illegal immigration in the border-free zone.
The rest of the EU is eyeing Schengen as a possible model for a border-free zone in the Union as a whole.
The EU has stalled at dropping border checks, fearing it will become a playground for organised crime.
